name: Bianca Tanaka

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Bianca. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a first-year apprentice on a city crew, working out of the Riverside depot. A lot of what we do is underground: opening up cable vaults under the pavement, replacing old joints, swapping transformers on the poles in the older streets. I'm the one on the ground running the pump, setting the barriers, handing tools down. My journeyman Dorota says I'm careful but slow, which is fair.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my partner Marco, who drives a parcel van, in a one-bedroom flat on the ring road. City rent eats most of what we make, and I've got maybe two weeks of savings. There's only one power company in the city, so if this doesn't work out, there's nowhere else to do this job without moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected. Some apps got a bit smarter and that's it. I wouldn't really bring it up at the depot.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it changes nothing, which isn't great either. The pressures are rent and low apprentice pay, and those don't change. It just means I keep grinding for three more years until I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going with the apprenticeship and try to save a bit from every pay packet. Marco and I would set up a separate savings account so we don't dip into it. And I'd keep using the chat tool now and then to help write the odd email to the landlord.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Not about AI, just about money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two weeks of savings in a city flat. What's the plan if the rent goes up again?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd probably have to find a cheaper flat further out, which means a longer commute to the depot. The landlord put the rent up last year by seventy a month. If the rent goes up again, we're stuck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does AI touch anything in your day now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Barely. Dorota uses one on her phone to look up regulations. I've used one to write a complaint to the landlord, that's about it.

say: I'd say it's **what I expected**: some apps got smarter.
I wouldn't really **bring it up** at the depot.
think: I think the **pressures** are rent and low pay, and those don't change.
I think I keep **grinding** for three years until I qualify.
do: I'd set up a **separate savings** account with my partner.
I'd keep using a **chat tool** now and then for emails to the landlord.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy**, but about **money**, not AI.
S0.quote: The landlord put the rent up last year by seventy a month. If the rent goes up again, we're stuck.
fieldNote: Her pressure is **city rent** on apprentice pay, not technology.
She's in a **one-employer city**, so leaving the job means moving.
She uses AI **occasionally**, mainly for writing emails.

steps.text: Open a separate savings account with Marco
Keep going with the city apprenticeship at the Riverside depot
Use a chat tool to write landlord emails

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big shift, but people adapt. Some office staff at the depot will go, which is sad, but that's how it goes. I'd keep my opinions mostly to myself online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own job, the cable vaults and joints, I think is safe for a good while. Robots can't easily climb into a flooded vault under the ring road. But the office planning would change, and I'd have to learn new apps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd learn the new planning app once a few others had tried it. I'd look into the cable jointing certificate, because it's a specialist skill and pays a bit more. I'd keep saving, even small amounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but okay. More worried for Marco than for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to Marco's job in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: His routes are already set by software, so not much changes for him yet. But his company keeps talking about vans that drive themselves. That's the one that keeps me up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the app once others had. Why wait?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because the first versions are always buggy. I'd let someone else find the bugs. Then I'd learn it properly.

say: I'd say it's a **big shift**, but people adapt.
I'd say losing some **office staff** at the depot is sad but normal.
think: I think **cable vault** work is safe for a good while.
I think office planning changes, so I'd need to learn **new apps**.
do: I'd learn the **planning app** once others had tried it.
I'd look into the **cable jointing** certificate and keep saving small amounts.
feel: I'd feel **uneasy but okay**, more worried for my partner than me.
S1.quote: Robots can't easily climb into a flooded vault under the ring road.
fieldNote: She sees **underground work** as hard to automate, giving her some safety.
Her worry shifts to her partner's **delivery job** and self-driving vans.
She's a **wait-then-learn** adopter: let others find the bugs first.

steps.text: Learn the new planning app after colleagues have tested it
Apply for the cable jointing certificate course
Save a small fixed amount from every pay packet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast, and people need time to adjust. I'd want some kind of support from the government, maybe a transition fund. But I'd be careful about what I say online.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it'd hit Marco first. Self-driving vans would come with the robots by 2031, and his job would go. My planning and paperwork would be done by AI, but I'd still be in the vaults for a few years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish my apprenticeship as fast as possible and get the jointing certificate. Marco and I would cut everything and start saving hard. We'd look at whether he could retrain into something like an electrician's mate with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed, I think. Two jobs at risk and two weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would happen to the flat if Marco's job went?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We couldn't afford the flat on my wage alone. We'd have to move to a cheaper area or move in with my sister. That's the honest answer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said robots can't get into a vault. Would you still believe that by 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe not. If robots can do hands-on work as well as people, someone will build one for vaults. I'd have a bit longer than Marco, that's all.

say: I'd say it's **too fast** and people need time.
I'd want a government **transition fund**, but I'd be careful online.
think: I think my partner's **delivery job** goes first with self-driving vans by 2031.
I think I'd stay in the **vaults** a bit longer than him.
do: I'd finish my **apprenticeship** fast and get the **jointing certificate**.
I'd cut everything and look at my partner **retraining** alongside me.
feel: I'd feel **alarmed**: two jobs at risk and two weeks of **savings**.
S2.quote: We couldn't afford the flat on my wage alone. We'd have to move to a cheaper area or move in with my sister.
fieldNote: She expects her **partner's job** to go, which makes the household mood alarmed.
She treats her own **vault work** as buying a few extra years, not safety.
The fallback is **family**: moving in with her sister.

steps.text: Fast-track the cable jointing certificate before 2028
Cut all spending except rent, food and travel
Move in with her sister if Marco's van job goes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning, and companies should use it. I'd talk to Dorota and the others about what training the company should offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be qualified with a jointing certificate by 2031. The robots come in 2034, so I'd have a few years as a specialist. Marco would have more time to find something new.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, get the jointing ticket, and start saving properly, a month at least. Marco would look at an electrician's course at the college. We'd hold off on any big spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less. Like there's time to get ready.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Marco do with five years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Marco would start the course in the evenings. We'd hold off on getting married until we know where we stand.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would make you feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A clear idea of which jobs are safe. If the power company told us straight what it planned, I'd feel better.

say: I'd say five years is a **decent warning** for companies to use.
I'd talk with colleagues about **training** the company should offer.
think: I think I'd be a **specialist** with a few years before robots arrive.
I think my partner would have **time** to find something new.
do: I'd qualify, get the **jointing ticket** and save at least a month.
I'd support my partner starting an **electrician's course** at the college.
feel: I'd feel **anxious but less**, with time to get ready.
S3.quote: If the power company told us straight what it planned, I'd feel better.
fieldNote: Five years gives the household a **two-person plan**: her ticket, his evening course.
She wants **straight talk** from the company about its plans.
She'd **delay marriage** until the picture is clearer.

steps.text: Qualify and get the cable jointing ticket by 2031
Save at least one month of expenses
Postpone the wedding until both jobs feel settled

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is enough time to prepare. I wouldn't be worried out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be a full lineworker with specialist skills, and maybe a team lead by 2036. The robots wouldn't come until 2039. I think I'd be okay, but I'd keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd qualify, specialise in jointing, and save steadily. Marco would retrain in the next few years. I'd use AI tools a bit more as they get proven at work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but calm enough.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years out. How does that change things for Marco?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd have time to switch, maybe to an electrician. He likes fixing things, so that's not a stretch.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your life look like in 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopefully married, with a small flat we own further out. I picture me running a jointing crew in the vaults and my partner Marco wiring houses. Not fancy, but steady.

say: I'd say ten years is **enough time** for everyone to prepare.
I'd tell people at the depot I'm **not worried**, at least out loud.
think: I think I'd be a **specialist**, maybe a team lead, by 2036.
I think I'd be okay but would **keep an eye** on it.
do: I'd specialise in **jointing** after qualifying and save a little every month.
I'd use **AI tools** more once they're proven at work.
S4.quote: I picture me running a jointing crew in the vaults and my partner Marco wiring houses. Not fancy, but steady.
fieldNote: Ten years gives both partners **time to switch**, easing the household risk.
Her hopes are **modest**: owning a small flat, a steady crew job.
She'd adopt **AI tools** once proven, as before.

steps.text: Specialise in underground cable jointing after qualifying
Save steadily towards a deposit on a small flat
Use AI tools at work once they're proven

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Marco and I could both lose work, and we've got two weeks of savings. What would help is a transition fund for families like us, and the company being honest about its plans.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the city. If you lose your job in this city, you can't stay, because the rent's too high. It's not just a job, it's the whole life.

headlineQuote: If you lose your job in this city, you can't stay, because the rent's too high. It's not just a job, it's the whole life.
portrait: Bianca is a **first-year apprentice** on a city crew, working underground in cable vaults.
She shares a **one-bedroom flat** with her partner Marco, a parcel van driver, and has two weeks saved.
She's **centrist** and careful about speaking up online.
She adopts tech **once proven**, and plans a cable jointing specialism.
She's uneasy in milder pictures and **alarmed** under fast AGI, mostly for her partner's job.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because **both jobs** could go with two weeks saved.
whatWouldHelp: The company being **honest** about its plans.
